entries.answer: Android is the operating system that runs on the majority of the world's phones, and the detail that shapes everything about it is that it is licensed to manufacturers rather than sold by one company. The source code is published, each manufacturer adapts it for its own hardware and adds its own interface on top, and that is why two Android phones from different brands can behave quite differently while still running the same applications. Applications are written in a managed language, compile down to bytecode that a runtime executes, and are distributed as a package containing the code, the resources and a manifest declaring the permissions the app wants. The system is built on a Linux kernel and sandboxes each app, so one app normally cannot read the files of another, and recent versions ask again for sensitive access rather than deciding it once at install. The main complaints are update fragmentation, where support for a given model ends at whatever the manufacturer chose, and the number of pre-installed applications that cannot be fully removed.

patterns: how do apps get on phones
why does an app need so much storage
entries.answer: An app store is the marketplace through which software is distributed to phones, and the store model is what turned the phone from a device with a fixed feature set into a general computer. The provider hosts the applications, handles discovery, payment, updates and in some regions review, so software reaches a phone without the user copying files around, and because updates are pushed centrally a fix can reach millions of devices in days. Each listing carries a minimum operating system version, which is how old devices end up unable to run anything new even though the hardware is not broken, and the accumulated size of applications is what fills the storage people then delete photos to free. The economics run on a commission taken from sales, which is why developers tend to offer things free with a paid upgrade rather than a plain price, and why the storefronts that allow alternative payment methods are such a contested area. For a user the practical facts are the same everywhere: an app asks for permissions, and the decision to grant them is the real contract.

patterns: how long does a phone battery last
why does my phone die fast
entries.answer: A phone battery is a rechargeable lithium ion cell, and its life is governed by capacity in milliamp hours together with how much power the device actually draws while you use it. The display is usually the largest single consumer, which is why brightness, refresh rate and screen size are the settings people are told to lower, and the other large draws are the radio, the camera and any app that keeps location active in the background. Charging follows a curve rather than being a simple fill: a lithium cell is stressed by sitting at a very high charge, so phones typically charge quickly to about 80 percent and then taper, and the overnight-to-full habit is what the charger manages. Heat shortens lifespan more than the number of cycles does, so leaving a phone in a hot car is worse than charging it often. Battery health in the system settings refers to the maximum capacity the cell can now hold compared with when it was new, and it is the number that predicts whether the day will still last.

patterns: is a touchscreen capacitive or resistive
why did my screen stop working
entries.answer: A touchscreen is a display that senses input from a finger or a stylus, and the technology underneath it is what makes a phone feel direct. The capacitive approach, used in essentially every modern phone, senses the change in capacitance of a grid of electrodes when a conductor touches it, and because the human body is conductive it works without pressure. That is the difference from the resistive screens before it, which needed a firm stylus and a two-layer film, and the durability improvement is a large part of why the older approach disappeared. A digitiser then converts the touch point into coordinates, and the operating system's software decides what that means, so the same panel can scroll one interface and tap another. The real limitations are practical rather than technical: water and gloves interfere with capacitive sensing, and because the screen is glass and the digitiser sits under it, a badly cracked display often cannot be replaced without the whole assembly.
